question.en: In a 2D side-scroller, why do far background layers scroll slower?

options: To save GPU memory on big images
To fake depth through parallax
To keep the HUD from overlapping
To stop the camera from jittering

explanation.en: Distant layers moving less than near ones mimics how far objects shift less as you move, giving a flat scene a sense of depth.

question.en: What are invincibility frames (i-frames)?

options: Frames dropped to keep up the frame rate
A brief window where hits are ignored
Keyframes where an attack deals damage
The opening frames before input is read
answer: A brief window where hits are ignored

explanation.en: After taking a hit or during a dodge, the character briefly cannot be damaged, which stops one attack from landing many times in a row.

question.en: How does a sprite sheet animate a 2D character?

options: By bending a skeleton under the sprite
By morphing between two vertex sets
By showing its frames one after another
By rotating a single image around a pivot
answer: By showing its frames one after another

explanation.en: A sprite sheet packs every frame into one texture; the game swaps which region it draws at a set rate, like a flipbook.

question.en: What visual problem does anti-aliasing reduce?

options: Screen tearing during camera pans
Jagged, stair-stepped edges
Blurry textures at a distance
Flicker between overlapping faces

explanation.en: Edges rasterised onto a pixel grid look stepped; MSAA, FXAA and TAA blend edge pixels to smooth them.

question.en: What is a decal in a 3D game?

options: A low-poly stand-in for a far mesh
A quad that always faces the camera
A texture projected onto surfaces
A baked shadow under a character

explanation.en: Decals project details such as bullet holes, scorch marks or graffiti onto existing geometry without changing its mesh or texture.

question.en: In animation, what is "anticipation"?

options: A wind-up before the main action
Looping a clip once it has finished
Easing out at the end of a move
Playing a clip slightly faster
answer: A wind-up before the main action

explanation.en: A small opposite movement, like crouching before a jump, tells the player what is about to happen and makes the action read clearly.

question.en: Why do fast action games usually send state over UDP rather than TCP?

options: UDP encrypts every packet by default
A lost packet does not stall later ones
UDP guarantees that packets arrive in order
TCP cannot cross home routers at all
answer: A lost packet does not stall later ones

explanation.en: TCP holds back newer data until a lost packet is resent, causing stalls; with UDP the game simply uses the next, more recent update.

question.en: What defines the shape of a cubic Bezier curve?

options: A centre point and a radius
Two angles and a speed value
Four control points
One point and a surface normal

explanation.en: The curve starts at the first point and ends at the fourth; the middle two pull it into shape without usually lying on it.

question.en: What does dead reckoning do for a remote player?

options: Rewinds them to the time of a shot
Extrapolates from their last velocity
Interpolates between two past snapshots
Hides them when packets are lost

explanation.en: Between updates, the client projects the entity forward from its last known position and velocity, then corrects when real data arrives.

question.en: How does a utility AI decide what to do next?

options: Follows a fixed sequence of states
Plans a whole chain of actions to a goal
Scores each option and picks the best
Picks an action uniformly at random
answer: Scores each option and picks the best

explanation.en: Each candidate action gets a score from curves over inputs like health or distance, and the agent chooses the highest-scoring one.

question.en: Why use a flow field when a huge crowd heads for one goal?

options: Units avoid each other for free
One grid serves every unit
Each unit gets a unique path
It removes the need for a map

explanation.en: A single pass from the goal stores a direction in every cell, so any number of units just follow the arrow under them instead of each running A*.

question.en: What does SSAO add to a rendered scene?

options: Reflections of on-screen objects
Darkening in creases and corners
Hard shadows cast by the sun
Light scattering through fog

explanation.en: Screen-space ambient occlusion samples the depth buffer around each pixel to estimate how enclosed it is, darkening crevices and contact areas.

question.en: In Phong-style lighting, what does the specular term model?

options: Light bounced from other surfaces
Colour of the surface in shadow
Shiny highlights from the light
Soft light scattered under skin

explanation.en: Specular depends on the view and light directions and produces the bright highlight on glossy surfaces; diffuse handles the matte part.

question.en: How do cellular automata turn random noise into caves?

options: A random walker carves out the tunnels
Rooms are split with a binary tree
Tiles follow adjacency constraints
Cells flip based on neighbour counts
answer: Cells flip based on neighbour counts

explanation.en: Each pass makes a cell solid or empty depending on how many neighbours are solid, so scattered noise smooths into organic cave walls.

question.en: Why offer a colourblind mode in a game?

options: To make it run on older monitors and TVs
So colour-coded info stays readable
To cut the GPU cost of colour
To shrink texture memory use

explanation.en: Swapping palettes or adding shapes and icons lets players who cannot tell certain hues apart still read team colours, warnings and rarity.

question.en: Why route sounds through mixer groups (buses)?

options: To make each sound play in 3D
To compress clips on import
To set volume per category at once
To loop music tracks without any gap
answer: To set volume per category at once

explanation.en: Grouping music, SFX and dialogue into buses lets volume sliders, ducking and effects apply to a whole category in one place.

question.en: Why leave spare room in UI layouts for translated text?

options: Fonts render a lot larger on consoles
Other languages often run longer
Translations add extra buttons
Screen readers need the spacing

explanation.en: Text in languages such as German or French is often noticeably longer than English, so tight labels would clip or overflow.

question.en: With these weights, how often does "rare" drop?

options: 1 in 70 rolls
25% of the time
5% of the time
1 in 3 rolls

explanation.en: The weights total 100, so each one is its share of the total: rare gets 5 / 100 = 5% of rolls.

question.en: What does goal-oriented action planning (GOAP) do?

options: Picks the single highest-scoring action
Runs a fixed tree of priority nodes
Searches for an action chain to a goal
Follows one scripted state per animation
answer: Searches for an action chain to a goal

explanation.en: Actions declare preconditions and effects, and a planner (often A*) searches for the cheapest sequence that turns the current world state into the goal.

question.en: Why split the view into cascaded shadow maps?

options: To let each cascade use a different light
To spend shadow resolution near the camera
To render each light in its own separate pass
To blur shadow edges at a distance
answer: To spend shadow resolution near the camera

explanation.en: One shadow map over a large view gives blurry near shadows; cascades give nearby slices of the frustum their own map with far more texels per metre.

question.en: What is the stencil buffer typically used for?

options: Storing per-pixel surface normals
Holding depth for shadow maps
Masking which pixels may be drawn
Caching the previous frame image
answer: Masking which pixels may be drawn

explanation.en: Draws can write reference values to the stencil and later draws test against them, enabling portals, outlines, mirrors and masked UI.

question.en: How does wave function collapse generate a level?

options: Carves rooms by splitting space in two
Picks tiles that satisfy adjacency rules
Smooths random noise into organic cave walls
Adds up octaves of noise into heights
answer: Picks tiles that satisfy adjacency rules

explanation.en: Each cell starts with every tile possible; the most constrained cell is collapsed to one tile and the neighbour rules propagate, repeating until all cells are fixed.

question.en: In position Verlet integration, where does velocity come from?

options: The current and previous positions
A velocity stored on each body
The collision normal each step
The force that was applied in the last frame

explanation.en: Verlet stores no explicit velocity; it is implied by the difference between this and the previous position, which makes constraints simple to apply.

question.en: Why can explicit Euler integration make a stiff spring explode?

options: It ignores the mass of the body
It only runs once per frame
Its error adds energy each step
It rounds positions to integers
answer: Its error adds energy each step

explanation.en: Explicit Euler uses the old velocity for the whole step, which systematically overshoots oscillators; with a stiff spring the gained energy grows until it blows up.

question.en: What does premultiplied alpha fix when blending textures?

options: Dark fringes on filtered edges
The need to sort transparency
Texture compression artefacts
Gaps between tiles in an atlas

explanation.en: Filtering straight-alpha texels blends in the colour of fully transparent pixels, often black; premultiplying weights colour by alpha first, so edges stay clean.
